title: Memory recall
description: Read-only recall over the engine's memory ledger — the project's narrative "how did I get here?" record (past decisions, the pushback and rationale behind them, lessons, dead-ends, preferences, intents). Every conforming implementation answers the same recall operation, so a session can ask "what do we already know about this?" and get the relevant past episodes ranked best-first, without knowing whether the offline keyword floor or a richer meaning-based engine is answering. It returns narrative recall only and never structural fact (knowledge's job); a caller that wants the entities a memory references composes that itself by filtering on an entity-id tag at read time.

operations.name: search
operations.description: Recall the memory records most relevant to a query, ranked best-first. An optional role filter narrows to record kinds (the closed memory role vocabulary: decision, rationale/pushback, lesson, dead-end, preference, intent, observation); an optional tag filter narrows to records carrying given tags (entity references such as eADR-#### or free topic tags — the read-time link to knowledge is composed by filtering on an entity-id tag); an optional limit caps how many results are returned.

query.description: The recall query text, matched against the records' narrative content.

roles.description: Restrict to these record roles (the closed memory role vocabulary: decision, rationale/pushback, lesson, dead-end, preference, intent, observation). Omit for all roles. Validated against the implementation's own role schema, not frozen by this contract.

tags.description: Restrict to records carrying any of these tags (entity references such as 'eADR-0007' or free topic tags). Omit for no tag filter.

limit.description: The maximum number of ranked results to return. Omit for the implementation's default.

results.description: The matching memory records, ordered best-first by relevance (the ranking is the implementation's — BM25 for the lexical floor, reinforced by usage). Each result is a record object whose exact shape is the memory substrate's own (role, narrative, tags, provenance, score), not frozen by this contract.

recall_completeness.description: An optional plain-language note, present only when results are returned, telling the reader the results are curated summaries whose original word-for-word notes are still kept and recoverable — so the reader can offer the operator the exact wording. Omitted when there are no results. Whether the note is present is not frozen by this contract; the completeness disclosure floor itself is enforced elsewhere, not by this key.

operations.name: recall-window
operations.description: Read back the actual conversation of one past session — the exact user and assistant turns, in the order they happened. The companion to `search`: search ranks and names a relevant session, this reads that session's own record rather than a summary of it, so exact wording is recoverable. It fetches and never ranks — ordering is the conversation's own, so this adds no second ranking to the contract. An optional anchor centres the window on one message with a radius either side, and a cap bounds how many turns come back. Read-only: reading a conversation changes nothing.

session_id.description: The session to read, as carried on a search result. A cross-session gist's session field is a cluster key (an implementation-specific sentinel) rather than a real session, so a caller resolves it to real sessions through that record's own source references first.

anchor_seq.description: Centre the window on the message with this ordinal. Note what a caller can actually supply: ranked results are summaries and carry no position within a conversation, so this is normally omitted on a first read and used on a follow-up, once an earlier window has shown which ordinals exist. Omit to read from the start.

radius.description: How many turns to include either side of the anchor. Ignored when no anchor is given. Omit for the implementation's default.

max_turns.description: How many turns to return at most, so a long session cannot flood the caller. A request above the implementation's own ceiling is clamped to it rather than honoured — the bound is the implementation's, not the caller's. Omit for the default.

session_id.description: The session that was asked for, echoed back as given.

sessions.description: The real sessions actually read. Normally the one asked for; when the request named a cluster key for a summary folded from several sessions, the implementation resolves it and this names what it resolved to. Empty when nothing could be resolved.

turns.description: The conversation turns in the order they happened, best-effort rejoined where the implementation stored one long message in pieces. Each turn is an object whose exact shape is the memory substrate's own (who spoke, the wording, its ordinal), not frozen by this contract. Empty when the session holds no readable conversation.

total.description: How many turns the session holds in all, so a caller can tell a capped window from a complete one.

returned.description: How many turns this answer carries.

truncated.description: True when the window was capped and the session holds more than was returned.

note.description: A plain-language note about this answer. When turns are returned it is the completeness caveat: the wording is reconstructed from what remains stored, and an implementation cannot in general prove no part of a long message was permanently erased. When no turns are returned it says WHY, so a caller can tell an unresolvable id from a session holding nothing readable, rather than reading silence as 'memory does not hold it'. Its exact wording is not frozen by this contract.
